interview_metadata.name: David Mckethan
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Raleigh, but I was raised mostly around Angier, North Carolina, and that is still home to me. I grew up in a Black Southern family where church, food, music, and helping neighbors were just part of regular life. My mama worked in a school cafeteria and my daddy drove deliveries for a building supply place, so I learned early that work was not always fancy, but it had dignity if you did it right. We went to a Baptist church most Sundays, and I remember choir rehearsals, homecomings, fish fries, and my aunties talking over each other in the kitchen. I was not a bad student, but I was the kind who liked hands-on things and people more than sitting still with a textbook. After high school I took some community college classes, then life and bills got in the way, and I started working retail full time. I met my wife, Tonya, through church friends in my twenties, and we built a life here with two kids. I have spent a lot of years as a cashier, and I have gotten good at it: counting a drawer quick, calming down a frustrated customer, training new hires, knowing when the milk delivery is late before the manager even asks. Lately I have gone back to school part time for business administration because I want to move up into shift lead or assistant manager, and someday I would like to open a small neighborhood convenience store or coffee kiosk. The big events in my life have mostly been family things: getting married, becoming a father, losing my father a few years back, and learning that worry can run you if you do not get a handle on it.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood in Angier, what are the clearest scenes that come back to you?
follow_ups.response: Summer evenings outside after supper, somebody grilling, cousins running through the yard, and gospel music or old soul playing from a radio. Also the county fair, church picnics, and older folks telling stories about what they had lived through.

follow_ups.question: What kind of student were you in high school?
follow_ups.response: I was steady but not top of the class. I did better when a teacher connected the lesson to real life, like business math or shop-type projects, and I liked being around people more than being quiet at a desk.

follow_ups.question: How did becoming a father change you?
follow_ups.response: It made me more careful with money and time. Once my daughter was born, I started thinking less about what I wanted that week and more about what the house needed six months from then.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: One crossroads was when I first dropped out of community college years ago. I had been taking classes, but I was working, trying to help at home, and then Tonya and I were getting serious. I could have tried to push through school, or I could work more hours and bring money in right away. I chose work because it felt responsible at the time. For a while I wondered if that choice boxed me in, but I also learned the retail business from the ground up. Now, going back to school in my forties, I see that old choice differently. It slowed me down, but it did not end the road. It gave me the practical side, and now I am trying to add the paper credentials.

follow_ups.question: What made you decide to return to school now?
follow_ups.response: I got tired of training people who then moved ahead of me because they had more formal education. I also want my kids to see that finishing something matters even if you finish later than planned.

follow_ups.question: Who encouraged you at that crossroads?
follow_ups.response: My wife did, even back then. She never made me feel small about working retail, but she always told me I had manager sense and should not stop learning.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. I made a conscious choice to work more hours, but the pressure built up little by little until it felt like the only practical thing to do.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel like sacrifice at the time?
follow_ups.response: A little, but mostly it felt like being grown. The regret came later when promotions started asking for school or management background.

follow_ups.question: Would you advise your children differently?
follow_ups.response: I would tell them to work if they need to, but keep school connected somehow, even one class at a time.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. Better advising at the community college would have helped, and maybe more flexible class times. I did not know how to ask for help back then.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Somebody laying out a part-time path that fit retail hours, and maybe help with books or transportation.

follow_ups.question: Did your employer support school at all?
follow_ups.response: Not really back then. Now there is more talk about training, but tuition help is still limited.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Tonya, and she is the center of the house in a lot of ways. She works as a medical receptionist in Fuquay-Varina, so she is organized, calm, and better than me at keeping appointments straight. We have two children at home: Maya, who is fifteen, and Caleb, who is ten. Maya is serious about school and sings some with the youth choir, though she pretends she is too cool for it sometimes. Caleb is all motion, basketball, video games, and asking for snacks five minutes after dinner. My mother, Evelyn, lives not too far away, and I check on her a few times a week. My father passed away, and I still hear his voice when I am trying to decide whether to spend money or fix something myself. Family for me also includes cousins, church folks, and a few neighbors who have been around so long they might as well be kin.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal family evening look like in your house?
follow_ups.response: If I am on an earlier shift, I get home around six, help with dinner or homework, and we eat together if everybody's schedule lets us. Later I may work on school assignments or watch a game with Caleb.

follow_ups.question: How do you and Tonya divide responsibilities?
follow_ups.response: Tonya handles a lot of appointments and school communication. I handle groceries, grilling, yard stuff, and getting the kids to practices when my work schedule allows.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your mother?
follow_ups.response: Usually two or three times a week, even if it is just dropping by after work or taking her a plate on Sunday.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have an older sister, Denise, in Raleigh. We talk every week or so, and she is the one who tells me straight when I am overthinking something.

follow_ups.question: Do you visit each other often?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a month, more around birthdays and holidays.

follow_ups.question: What is she like compared with you?
follow_ups.response: She is sharper with paperwork and planning. I am more easygoing with people day to day.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are from church, work, and basketball. There is Marcus, who I play pickup ball with on Saturdays, and Andre, who has known me since high school. At church I am close with our choir director, Sister Janice, because we spend Thursday nights getting everybody ready for Sunday. At work I mentor a younger cashier named Luis, and we have gotten close because he asks questions and reminds me of myself starting out.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see those friends?
follow_ups.response: Marcus and the basketball group are usually weekly. Church folks I see Thursday and Sunday, and work friends depend on the schedule.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your friends usually do together?
follow_ups.response: Basketball, cookouts, watching Hornets games, or just standing by the grill talking about work, kids, and bills.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Angier, in a modest neighborhood where people know each other's cars and kids. It is not fancy, but it has porches, yards, church signs, small stores, and enough quiet that you can hear somebody mowing on a Saturday morning. We are close enough to Fuquay-Varina and Raleigh for work or shopping, but Angier still feels like a small town. People wave, ask after your mama, and show up with food when somebody passes. At the same time, costs have gone up, and you can feel the area changing as more people move outward from the bigger towns.

follow_ups.question: Where do people in the neighborhood gather?
follow_ups.response: Church events, the park, cookouts, school games, and sometimes just somebody's driveway on a weekend.

follow_ups.question: What changes have you noticed recently?
follow_ups.response: More traffic, more new houses, and higher grocery and rent prices. It still feels like home, but it is not as cheap as it used to be.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. We have occasional car break-ins and some late-night foolishness, but I know my neighbors and that helps.

follow_ups.question: Do you let your kids move around the neighborhood freely?
follow_ups.response: Caleb can ride his bike nearby, but I want to know where he is. Maya has more freedom, but we still check in by phone.

follow_ups.question: What makes you feel safe?
follow_ups.response: Knowing who belongs, neighbors watching out, and people calling each other before calling anybody else.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is community, family history, and being close to church. The downside is fewer job ladders nearby and having to drive for better pay, doctors, or certain stores.

follow_ups.question: Have you thought about moving?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but our roots are here. If we moved, it would probably still be within driving distance.

follow_ups.question: What would improve Angier for your family?
follow_ups.response: More youth programs, better sidewalks, and more small businesses owned by local people.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my wife Tonya, our daughter Maya, and our son Caleb. We all live there full time. My mother does not live with us, but she is close by, and my sister or cousins may stay over after a family event once in a while. The household rhythm is busy but steady: work, school, choir, basketball, homework, and meals.

follow_ups.question: Who is usually home first on weekdays?
follow_ups.response: Usually the kids, depending on school activities, then Tonya, then me if I am on a later shift.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids share household chores?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Maya helps with dishes and laundry, and Caleb takes trash out and feeds the dog when we are watching my mother's dog.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone in the household is permanent.

follow_ups.question: No one staying for work or school right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been the four of us for years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my niece stays over after visiting with Maya, but it is occasional.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two.

follow_ups.question: Is it usually planned?
follow_ups.response: Most of the time, yes, around family gatherings.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody who usually lives with us is away.

follow_ups.question: Any college students away from home?
follow_ups.response: No, our kids are still at home.

follow_ups.question: Any long hospital stays in the household?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully not.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week depends on the store schedule. Some days I open and I am up before 5:30, making coffee, checking on the kids' lunches, and getting to work early enough to count in. Other days I work mid-shift or close, so mornings are for schoolwork, errands, or checking on my mother. Thursdays are choir rehearsal in the evening. Saturdays often mean pickup basketball in the morning, then yard work or grilling if the weather is right. Sundays are church, family meal, and trying to reset before Monday.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: On a good night around 10:30, but if I am worried about bills or doing schoolwork, it can be midnight.

follow_ups.question: Which day feels busiest?
follow_ups.response: Thursday, because work, dinner, homework checking, and choir all run together.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a cashier at a local retail and convenience store. My main duties are running the register, handling cash, helping customers, stocking when we are slow, checking inventory, and training newer staff on the POS system. I usually work about 38 to 40 hours a week, with some weekends. The schedule changes, but I often have either a 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. shift or a 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. shift. I am trying to show I can handle shift-lead responsibilities, so I help close drawers and solve customer issues even when it is not officially my title.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job are you best at?
follow_ups.response: Keeping a line moving without making people feel rushed. I can count change, scan fast, and still remember somebody's usual brand of coffee.

follow_ups.question: What is the hardest part?
follow_ups.response: Unpredictable schedules and customers taking out their bad day on the person behind the counter.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I am taking business administration classes part time at the community college, mostly online with some evening requirements. I also help lead the church choir, so I pick songs, practice harmonies, and call people when we need extra voices for Sunday. At home I do grocery runs, a lot of the grilling and weekend cooking, and I keep an eye on the family budget. I also check in on my mother and help with small repairs at her place.

follow_ups.question: When do you fit schoolwork in?
follow_ups.response: Usually early mornings on late-shift days or after the kids go to bed.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep a written budget?
follow_ups.response: Yes, partly in a notebook and partly on my phone. I like seeing what is due before it sneaks up on me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is school. Adding classes has made me more careful with my evenings, and I have had to say no to some extra hanging out. Work has also been short-staffed, so I have been called in more often. Maya has more school activities now, and Caleb's basketball practices changed times, so Tonya and I do a lot of calendar juggling.

follow_ups.question: Has the new routine affected your sleep?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially during assignment weeks. I can stay up worrying or trying to finish something after a closing shift.

follow_ups.question: What helps you keep it organized?
follow_ups.response: Phone reminders, Tonya's calendar on the fridge, and Sunday night planning.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Maya gets up around 6:15, gets herself ready, and catches the bus or rides with Tonya depending on the day. She stays after sometimes for choir or school clubs. Caleb needs more pushing in the morning; he eats cereal, hunts for his shoes, and gets to school around 7:45. After school he has basketball practice a couple days a week or plays outside. Evenings are homework, dinner, showers, and trying to get them off screens before bed.

follow_ups.question: Who helps with homework?
follow_ups.response: Tonya does more of the language arts and school emails, and I help with math or projects.

follow_ups.question: What are weekends like for them?
follow_ups.response: Chores first, then basketball, church, cousins, and sometimes a movie night at home.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have been mixed. I have never been arrested, but I have had traffic stops where I felt like I had to be extra calm and careful because I am a Black man in the South. One time I was stopped coming home late from work, and the officer asked too many questions for a simple taillight issue. I keep my hands visible, speak respectfully, and tell my kids the same. I also know a couple officers through community events, so I do not put everybody in one box.

follow_ups.question: What did you tell your children about those situations?
follow_ups.response: I tell them to be respectful, keep their hands where they can be seen, and call us as soon as they can. It is a sad conversation, but I think it is necessary.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable calling police if needed?
follow_ups.response: If there is danger, yes. For smaller disputes, I would rather start with neighbors or church folks if that is possible.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: At community events, I have seen officers be helpful with traffic and kids. But I also remember being followed in a store as a teenager and feeling like suspicion was already on me.

follow_ups.question: Did that teenage experience stay with you?
follow_ups.response: Yes. It taught me early that being polite does not always stop somebody from assuming the worst.

follow_ups.question: Have things improved locally?
follow_ups.response: Some relationships are better, but trust still depends on the person and the situation.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not been arrested. I had a cousin arrested years ago over a drug-related charge, and it hurt the family because once that record followed him, work got harder.

follow_ups.question: Are you still close with that cousin?
follow_ups.response: We talk at family events. He has worked hard to get steady, but it has not been easy.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape how you think about the system?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I believe in accountability, but I also see how hard it is for people to come back after one mistake.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote most of the time, especially presidential elections and local races when I know what is on the ballot. I have missed a smaller election before when work and family got hectic, but I try not to. My parents and church elders always talked about voting like it was paid for by somebody else's struggle, so I carry that with me. I pay more attention now because school boards, town decisions, and policing affect my kids directly.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide who to vote for locally?
follow_ups.response: I look at schools, jobs, roads, small business, and whether they actually show up in communities like ours.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but not yelling. Tonya and I talk through ballots, and we try to explain issues to the kids in plain language.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I lean Democratic, but I am practical more than loud about a party. I care about working people, affordable health care, public schools, fair policing, and small business opportunity. I do not like politicians who only come around during campaign season and then forget rural towns and Black neighborhoods. I believe people should work hard, but I also know hard work does not mean much if wages are too low, rent is too high, or a medical bill wipes you out. My church background makes me value family and responsibility, but it also makes me believe we are supposed to help the stranger and the neighbor. I am cautious about government waste, but I do think government has a role when regular families cannot get a fair shake.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Health care costs and wages. I see working people every day who are doing their best and still counting every dollar.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever vote for Republicans?
follow_ups.response: I have considered it locally if the person seemed serious and respectful, but most of the time the Democratic candidate lines up better with my priorities.

follow_ups.question: What political talk turns you off?
follow_ups.response: Name-calling, culture-war noise, and people acting like poverty is just laziness.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten more focused on local politics. When I was younger, I thought mainly about presidents and big national issues. Now I pay attention to school boards, town development, traffic, police accountability, and whether small businesses can survive. COVID and inflation also made me think more about how fragile families' finances are. I am still moderate in how I talk, but I am less patient with leaders who pretend everything is fine.

follow_ups.question: What made local politics feel more important?
follow_ups.response: Having kids in school and seeing Angier grow. Decisions about roads, zoning, and schools show up in daily life.

follow_ups.question: Has your wife influenced your views?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Working in a medical office, she sees what insurance and appointment access do to people, and that has sharpened my thinking.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me a lot, though I did not need the news to tell me racism existed. Seeing those videos and hearing people argue over whether Black lives should be treated with basic dignity was heavy. It made me think about my son growing up and how soon we have to teach him things other kids may not have to learn. I supported the message, though I am not the type who is at every protest. For me it became more conversations at home, at church, and with friends.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend any protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one local peaceful gathering, more of a prayer and community event than a march.

follow_ups.question: How did Caleb respond?
follow_ups.response: He was young, so we kept it simple. We told him some people are treated unfairly and that we want him safe and proud of who he is.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about accountability, dignity, and the feeling of always having to prove you are not a threat. I do not think every officer is bad, but I do think systems can protect bad behavior too easily. I also think people get uncomfortable when Black folks talk honestly about fear, history, and daily disrespect. In church, we talked about justice and peace needing to go together. To me, the issue is not about hating police; it is about wanting my family treated fairly.

follow_ups.question: What would accountability look like to you?
follow_ups.response: Clear consequences, body camera transparency, better training, and departments listening before something bad happens.

follow_ups.question: Do you think the conversation has changed anything?
follow_ups.response: Some awareness changed, but I am not sure enough policy changed. People move on fast.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we are still carrying history even when people say they are tired of hearing about it. In rural North Carolina, you can see both progress and old patterns. My kids have opportunities my grandparents did not have, but they also hear comments, see who gets followed in stores, and notice whose neighborhoods get investment. I try to teach pride without teaching bitterness. That is a balance: knowing the truth, but not letting it steal your joy.

follow_ups.question: How do you teach your children that balance?
follow_ups.response: We talk about history, we celebrate Black music and family stories, and we tell them to carry themselves with confidence.

follow_ups.question: Where do you see progress?
follow_ups.response: More interracial friendships, more Black professionals visible to kids, and more people willing to talk openly.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family, church friends, and coworkers. I went to one peaceful local gathering, but mostly my response has been conversations and teaching my kids.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I share something thoughtful, but I avoid arguing in comment sections.

follow_ups.question: Are conversations at work different from church conversations?
follow_ups.response: Yes. At church people speak more openly; at work I choose my words carefully.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Tonya is very protective and practical; she wants change, but she also worries about safety. My sister Denise is more outspoken and posts more online. Some church elders connect it to civil rights stories from their parents. My basketball friends talk about it straight, especially when somebody has had a traffic stop. There are also a few people around town who get tired of the topic, but in my close circle most folks understand why it matters.

follow_ups.question: Do your children hear adults discuss it?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but we try to make sure they also hear hope, not just fear.

follow_ups.question: Has it caused conflict with anyone?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly online acquaintances. I usually step away before it turns ugly.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is decent, but I need to do better. I am on my feet at work, and I play basketball, so I am not inactive. But I carry some extra weight, my blood pressure has been a little high at checkups, and stress can mess with my sleep. My knees remind me I am not twenty-five anymore after pickup games. I am trying to drink more water, eat smaller portions, and not make every weekend a rib-and-mac-and-cheese event.

follow_ups.question: Do you take medication for blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: Not right now. The doctor told me to monitor it and work on diet and exercise first.

follow_ups.question: How often do you play basketball?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week, sometimes twice if the community center league has a game.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: The easy part is that I like moving when it feels social, like basketball or walking at a festival. The hard part is schedule, stress, and food. I know how to smoke ribs and make collards taste right, but healthy portions are another matter. Closing shifts also make it tempting to eat late or grab convenience food.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: Keeping water with me at work and cutting back on sodas.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest to change?
follow_ups.response: Late-night snacking after a stressful shift.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing major like surgery or a broken bone. The main thing was a checkup where my blood pressure was higher than the doctor liked, and that got my attention. I also had some knee pain after a basketball league game last winter, but it improved with rest, ice, and better shoes. The bigger health issue has been stress and sleep. I had a couple weeks where I woke up at 3 a.m. thinking about bills and school deadlines.

follow_ups.question: Did you follow up on the blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I went back a few months later, and it was a little better but still something to watch.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee pain affect work?
follow_ups.response: Only for a few days. Standing all day made it sore, so I wore a brace and slowed down on basketball.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working or caring for my kids, but fatigue and stress can make me short-tempered. Knee soreness can make a long shift feel longer.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work because of health?
follow_ups.response: Only a sick day here and there, nothing long-term.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when stress makes you irritable?
follow_ups.response: I try to step outside, pray, breathe, or put on music before I say something wrong.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, my mother's health is something I watch. She has diabetes and some arthritis, so I check whether she has groceries, whether she made her appointments, and whether she is moving around okay. Tonya is good about reminding me not to take it all on myself, but I worry. When my father was sick before he passed, that changed how I think about not waiting too long to see a doctor.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help does your mother need most?
follow_ups.response: Rides sometimes, help picking up prescriptions, small repairs, and somebody to listen when she is frustrated.

follow_ups.question: Does your sister help too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Denise helps with phone calls, paperwork, and coming down when she can.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have gotten care, but it can be expensive and inconvenient. My job has limited benefits, and Tonya's job helps some, but deductibles and copays still matter. There have been times I delayed a dental visit or a checkup because I did not want another bill. For the kids, we try not to delay anything important. Appointments can also mean missing work hours, and that is always a calculation.

follow_ups.question: What care have you most often delayed?
follow_ups.response: Dental work and routine follow-ups for myself.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a primary care clinic, though I do not go as often as I probably should.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?

follow_ups.response: An uncle did, but not me.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever consider it?
follow_ups.response: Briefly after high school, but I went into work instead.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Christian, Baptist.

follow_ups.question: Do you belong to a church?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a local Baptist church.

follow_ups.question: Are you active there?

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: I usually think of myself as a Democrat, but not blindly. I would say I am a moderate Democrat or a practical Democrat. I associate with the party because it lines up better with working families, health care, civil rights, and schools. But I still want candidates to earn the vote and talk about real local problems.

follow_ups.question: How strong is that identification?
follow_ups.response: Moderately strong. I know where I lean, but I still look at the person.

follow_ups.question: What would make you disappointed in Democrats?
follow_ups.response: If they ignore rural communities or only speak in slogans.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Closer to the Democratic Party.

follow_ups.question: Is that true nationally and locally?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, though locally I still look at the candidate.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from identifying as Republican?
follow_ups.response: Their positions on race, health care, wages, and voting rights usually do not fit me.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Angier, North Carolina.

follow_ups.question: Were you in the same general area as now?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: What was Angier like then?
follow_ups.response: Smaller, quieter, and more everybody-knows-everybody.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, I lived with both my mother and father.

follow_ups.question: Were they together then?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was the household stable?
follow_ups.response: Yes, strict sometimes, but stable.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My older sister Denise lived there too, though she was close to leaving for work and school by then.

follow_ups.question: Any grandparents in the home?
follow_ups.response: No, but they were nearby and involved.

follow_ups.question: Any cousins staying regularly?
follow_ups.response: Cousins were around a lot, but did not live there.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?

follow_ups.question: Any college or trade school?

follow_ups.response: Yes, very much.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: My mom completed high school.

follow_ups.question: Any later training?
follow_ups.response: Some food service and school workplace training.

follow_ups.question: Did she value education?
follow_ups.response: Absolutely. She pushed us to do more.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, she worked for pay.

follow_ups.question: Was she working when you were in high school?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was her schedule steady?
follow_ups.response: Mostly school-day hours.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked in a school cafeteria. She prepared food, served students, cleaned the kitchen area, kept food lines moving, and made sure kids who forgot lunch money were not embarrassed if she could help it.

follow_ups.question: Did she like the job?
follow_ups.response: She liked the children and the steady schedule, though the pay was not high.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape how you see service work?
follow_ups.response: Yes. She taught me service work deserves respect.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a public school cafeteria in Harnett County. The school educated children, and the cafeteria provided breakfast and lunch during the school day.

follow_ups.question: Was it close to home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, close enough that she knew many families.

follow_ups.question: Did people in town know her from that work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, plenty of former students still recognize her.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked for pay the whole time I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was he full time?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Did he have one main occupation?
follow_ups.response: Mostly delivery and warehouse work.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked as a delivery driver and warehouse worker for a building supply company. He loaded trucks, delivered materials, checked orders, kept inventory straight, and did a lot of physical lifting. He was reliable and knew how to fix almost anything.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from his work?
follow_ups.response: Show up on time, know your tools, and do not waste money replacing what you can repair.

follow_ups.question: Did he talk about work at home?
follow_ups.response: Some, usually about people not planning properly or a truck giving trouble.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for a building supply business that sold lumber, hardware, and materials to contractors and homeowners. They did not make the materials; they stocked, sold, and delivered them.

follow_ups.question: Was it a local company?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a local or regional business.

follow_ups.question: Did his job connect him to the community?
follow_ups.response: Yes. He knew contractors, farmers, church folks, and homeowners all over the area.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I have finished my associate degree and moved into a shift lead or assistant manager role. I want our family finances to feel less tight, with savings that can handle emergencies without panic. I hope Maya and Caleb are healthy, confident, and making good choices. I would like Tonya to have more breathing room too, because she carries a lot. Long term, I still picture a small store or coffee kiosk that feels like a community spot, with good coffee, basic groceries, maybe local pastries, and a bulletin board for church events and youth sports. I do not need to be rich. I want to be steady, respected, useful, and able to leave my kids a stronger foundation.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Finishing the degree and getting promoted at work.

follow_ups.question: What would your ideal store feel like?
follow_ups.response: Clean, friendly, music low in the background, people greeted by name, and prices fair.

follow_ups.question: What do you want to stay the same?
follow_ups.response: Our family closeness, church connection, and roots in the community.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, faith, community, and dignity in work. I value being the kind of man my children can trust and my wife can lean on. I value music, food, and gatherings because they remind people they are not alone. I also value resilience, especially the kind I saw in my parents and older Black folks in my community. To me, success is not just what you own; it is whether people feel better, safer, or more seen when they come around you.

follow_ups.question: What value do you most want your children to inherit?
follow_ups.response: Integrity. Do what you say, treat people right, and do not forget where you came from.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel most like yourself?
follow_ups.response: At the grill with family around, or in the choir when the song finally comes together.
